sections.title: Statistical Analysis for Political Science III
sections.description:
Contemporary social and political science are adopting new statistical methods at a dizzying rate. But recent developments have built from a few basic statistical frameworks which we aim to introduce in this course: causal inference and Bayesian inference. We can’t know what new methods the discipline will develop in the years to come. Still, it is likely they will build from these two foundational frameworks.
The course aims to familiarize students with these two statistical frameworks, including their core questions and foundational assumptions. At end, you will be able to rigorously evaluate the assumptions underpinning an estimate, and discuss in detail what assumptions are required for an estimate to be considered “causal.” You will also be familiar with the fundamentals of Bayesian inference, and with the wide variety of modeling possibilities that it enables. Our primary empirical applications in our Bayesian unit will be to problems of “text as data.”
Still, this is a course in applied statistics—and to that end, we will use problem sets to develop mastery over a variety of statistical techniques during the semester. This course aims to leave you better prepared to read and produce credible quantitative research in political and social science. Note that we cover a lot of ground—in an ideal world, each of these topics would get its own stand-alone, semester-length course.
